newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Ailing Yeltsin marks 100 days of second term.
newsitem.headline: Ailing Yeltsin marks 100 days of second term.

text.p: One hundred days into ailing President Boris Yeltsin's second term in office, commentators are divided over whether Russia is running well on auto-pilot as he waits for heart surgery or whether it is sliding into chaos.
The Kremlin chief's supporters say the lack of political storms since he was reelected on July 3 show he has created a system that is stable, even in his absence.
But critics say decision-making is frozen and Russia is in chaos.

Independent analysts say the reality may be somewhere in between. They agree upheaveals have been averted but fear inertia is setting in and that even Yeltsin's return after heart surgery would do little to kick the Kremlin into action.
Doctors will decide in the next few weeks when to operate on Yeltsin, 65, and say the normal recovery period for bypass surgery to improve blood supply to the heart to is up to two months.
"I think the first 100 days have shown that we have already entered the post-Yeltsin period," political analyst Andrei Kortunov, head of the Russian Science Foundation, told Reuters.

"Yeltsin will not come back as he once was. Even if the operation is successful, his age and general condition mean he will have to change his role and become the 'legitimiser', dealing with overall strategy rather than day-to-day governing."
Yeltsin's first 100 days since the election ended on Friday.
Aides say the president is still at the helm, even though he has so far spent much of his second term as president in hospital, on vacation or, as now, at a sanatorium.

The president has already handed some duties to Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and will temporarily give him all powers, including the "red button" controlling Russia's nuclear missiles, when he has the operation.

Most independent observers say Yeltsin still has a say in state affairs, but much of his power is now divided between Chernomyrdin, Kremlin chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais and, to a lesser extent, security tsar Alexander Lebed.
"Yeltsin's main achievement in the first 100 days has been to preserve his regime," said Sergei Markov, an analyst at the Moscow office of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.
"He does not have full control and does not make everyday decisions, but he has the final say in personnel appointments and over whether there is war or peace in Chechnya."
Yeltsin has worked hard to try to divide power among rival groups in the Kremlin to prevent anyone abusing it. Even the ambitious Lebed remains, despite threats to resign.
But some doubt Yeltsin has got the balance right and say the rivals are trying to usurp power.

"We have an unconstitutional regency while the president is alive," said Alexander Korzhakov, Yeltsin's confidant until his sacking in June as head of his personal security. "The president has fewer and fewer levers of power left in his hands."

The delicate balance of power Yeltsin has tried to create could be further upset by the political intrigues which, long simmering under the surface, burst into the open last week when former Kremlin aides traded charges of corruption.

It is all part of a complex power play in which Chubais, Chernomyrdin, Lebed and others are trying to consolidate their position for the next presidential election -- in four years if Yeltsin holds out but sooner if he is incapacitated.
For Chubais and Chernomyrdin, the aim is to prevent major changes, keep policy on track and hope Yeltsin recovers.

Chubais is widely unpopular and Chernomyrdin's ability to win an election is questionable. Opposition communist leader Gennady Zyuganov and Lebed would probably be better placed than them if an early election were called.
"Chernomyrdin and Chubais simply want to put an election off for as long as possible because Lebed is popular and they have real power now and don't want to lose it," Markov said.

Major factors in the power struggle in the coming weeks will be whether the opposition-dominated parliament forces a showdown with the government over its 1997 budget plans, whether peace holds in rebel Chechnya and whether labour unrest spreads.

The budget battle could undermine Chernomyrdin and Chubais, who is seen as his ally. Fighting in Chechnya could damage Lebed because he has signed a peace deal for the region and labour unrest would be the best ammunition for Zyuganov.
